title: In the seen, only the seen
hook: to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard

segments.voice: Yesterday: doubts vanish, three watches of the night under the tree. Your line: see one cause clearly. Today, a teaching only a few lines long, given on a city street.

On the coast at Supparaka lives a man called Bahiya of the bark cloth, because he dresses in strips of bark. People honor him and bring him food and robes; many think he's fully awakened. One day he wonders it himself. And a deity who wishes him well, the text says, tells him plainly: you're not, and you're not even on the way. But in Savatthi, far to the north, there's someone who is. Bahiya sets out at once; the text says he never stayed more than one night anywhere on the way. At the monastery he's told the Teacher has gone into town for alms. So he follows him into the street.
screen: `BAHIYA OF THE BARK CLOTH.` → `YOU'RE NOT EVEN ON THE WAY.` → `HE FOLLOWS HIM INTO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Bahiya finds the Buddha walking for alms, falls at his feet, and asks: teach me. It's not the time, the Buddha says; we've come into town for alms. Bahiya asks again, and gives his reason: life is uncertain, yours and mine. Not the time, the Buddha says again. A third time Bahiya asks. And there in the street, alms bowl in hand, the Buddha gives him a teaching only a few lines long. Train yourself like this, Bahiya. In the seen, there will be only the seen. In the heard, only the heard. In the sensed, only the sensed. In the known, only the known. When that's so, you won't be with it. When you're not with it, you won't be in it. Then you'll be neither here nor beyond nor in between. That is the end of suffering. Look at the first line. You see a face in a crowd, and instantly the mind adds: she's frowning at me, I must have done something, I always do this. The seen was a face. Everything else was added. The teaching asks Bahiya to stop at the face: not to stop seeing, but to stop building on top of it. When nothing is added, there's no I standing in the middle, taking it personally. Then the Buddha walks on with his bowl.
screen: `THREE TIMES HE ASKS.` · `IN THE STREET, WITH THE BOWL.` · `SEEN, HEARD, SENSED, KNOWN.` · `NOTHING ADDED, NO ONE IN THE MIDDLE.` · then, large: `IN THE SEEN, ONLY THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Rest your open eyes on something near you, a cup, a patch of wall, and let it be only what's seen: color, shape, light. When the mind adds a name, a story or an opinion, notice that it's added and come back. Then close your eyes and do the same with sound, letting a passing car be just a rising and falling sound.
Dittha, the seen. The Buddha's teaching to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; nothing added, and no one in the middle.
Your line: stop at the face. The rest of the story can wait. More of Bahiya tomorrow.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in Theravada and other traditions often give the Bahiya instruction as a practice of bare attention: noting what is seen, heard, sensed and known, without adding to it.

ask again, because life is uncertain.

original.note: Pali dittha: the seen. 'dittha ditthamattam': in the seen, only the seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the seen, only the seen means don't overthink.
what it means: stop at what the senses give; when nothing is added, there's no self standing in the middle to take it personally.
what a scholar hears: the four (dittha, suta, muta, vinnata: seen, heard, sensed, known) recur in the canon; the same instruction is given to Malunkyaputta in SN 35.95.
guess: the seen: just what meets the eye

chat.says: What did the Buddha mean, 'in the seen, only the seen'?
options: See what's there without adding a story on top, so no I is in the middle.
Stop looking at things, since seeing itself leads to suffering.
Trust only your eyes, and doubt anything you hear from others.
chat.meaning: The teaching asks Bahiya to stop at what is seen: not to stop seeing, but to stop building on top of it.

Bahiya.meaning: a seeker in bark cloth who traveled to meet the Buddha

Supparaka.meaning: the coastal town where Bahiya lived

Savatthi.meaning: the northern city where the Buddha was staying

notes: Udana 1.10 paraphrased. Confirm the deity is described as a former blood relative who wished him well (the script says only 'a deity who wishes him well').
'Tradition says he made the whole journey without stopping' (the commentary says in one night); confirm.
The face-in-the-crowd illustration is the writer's, not the text's.
